summary: Defines DHCPv6 options for passing a list of available recursive DNS name servers and a domain search list to a client. This lets a host learn which servers to ask for name lookups, without manual setup. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) hands a host its settings when it joins a network. This RFC adds two settings to that exchange: a list of DNS servers the host should ask, and a list of domain names to try when a name lookup fails. Without them, an administrator would have to configure every host by hand.

questions: how does dhcpv6 provide dns servers
how does a client get dns servers from dhcpv6
what is a domain search list
subtitle: Two DHCPv6 options that tell a host which DNS servers to use and which domain names to try.

tldr.problem: A host that gets its IPv6 address from DHCP still has to be told which DNS servers to ask and which domain names to try when it resolves a name.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two DHCPv6 options: option 23 carries a list of IPv6 addresses of recursive DNS servers in order of preference, and option 24 carries the domain search list, encoded as in RFC 3315.
tldr.outcome: Both options are restricted to a fixed set of DHCPv6 messages, and the RFC warns that a rogue DHCP server can abuse them to spoof DNS names, so clients are advised to require DHCP authentication.

today: RFC 3646 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. The two options it defines were originally part of the DHCPv6 specification in RFC 3315 and were split out into their own document.

sections.title: What the Two Options Do
sections.content:
This RFC defines two options for DHCPv6, the configuration protocol that lets a host on an IPv6 network get its address and its settings from a server. Both options carry Domain Name Service (DNS) information to the client.

The DNS Recursive Name Server option gives the client a list of one or more IPv6 addresses of DNS recursive name servers that its resolver may send queries to. The servers are listed in the order of preference for use by the client resolver. The Domain Search List option gives the client the list of domain names to try when it resolves a host name with DNS. It applies to DNS only, and not to other name resolution mechanisms.

Throughout the document, unless otherwise specified, the acronym DHCP refers to DHCP for IPv6 as specified in RFC 3315, and the terminology specific to IPv6 and DHCP defined in that document is used. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14, RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer joins an IPv6 network, DHCPv6 can tell it its address and other settings. This RFC adds two DNS-related settings to that handover: which DNS servers to ask, and which domain names to try when a lookup fails.

sections.title: The DNS Recursive Name Server Option
sections.content:
The option has a two-octet option code, OPTION_DNS_SERVERS, which is 23, followed by a two-octet option length. The option length gives the length of the list of DNS recursive name servers in octets, and it must be a multiple of 16, because each entry in the list is a 16-octet IPv6 address. The rest of the option is the list of those addresses.

A client's DNS resolver MAY send DNS queries to the servers on that list. The order in which the addresses appear is the order of preference for use by the client resolver, so the first entry is the one the resolver should try first.
sections.plainLanguage: This option is a list of IPv6 addresses. The list length must be a multiple of 16 bytes, since each server takes one IPv6 address. The servers are listed in the order the resolver should try them.

sections.title: The Domain Search List Option
sections.content:
This option has a two-octet option code, OPTION_DOMAIN_LIST, which is 24, followed by a two-octet option length giving the length of the searchlist field in octets. The searchlist field holds the list of domain names in the Domain Search List.

The list of domain names in the searchlist MUST be encoded as specified in the section on Representation and use of domain names of RFC 3315, which is the encoding DHCPv6 uses for domain names in its other options.

The option specifies the domain search list the client is to use when resolving hostnames with DNS. It does not apply to other name resolution mechanisms, so a client that resolves names in some other way, such as by consulting a local file, is unaffected by it.
sections.plainLanguage: This option holds the domain names to try, written in the same encoding DHCPv6 uses everywhere else for domain names. When the resolver looks up a short name, it can try each of these suffixes in turn.

sections.title: Which Messages Carry the Options
sections.content:
Both options are restricted to a fixed set of DHCPv6 messages, so that they are never exchanged in a context where they would not be understood.

The DNS Recursive Name Server option MUST NOT appear in any message other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply. The Domain Search List option MUST NOT appear in any message other than the same seven: Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The two options travel only in the DHCPv6 messages used to set up and refresh a lease. They must not appear in any other message type.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DNS Recursive Name Server option may be used by an intruder DHCP server to cause DHCP clients to send DNS queries to an intruder DNS recursive name server. The results of these misdirected queries may be used to spoof DNS names. To avoid attacks through this option, the DHCP client SHOULD require DHCP authentication before it installs a list of DNS recursive name servers obtained through authenticated DHCP.

The Domain Search List option may be used in the same way, to cause DHCP clients to search through invalid domains for incompletely specified domain names, and the results of these misdirected searches may be used to spoof DNS names. The RFC notes that support for DNSSEC will not avert this attack, because the resource records in the invalid domains may be legitimately signed.

How vulnerable a host is to an invalid domain search option is determined in part by DNS resolver behaviour. The RFC points to the recommendations in section 6 of RFC 1536: use search lists only when they are explicitly specified, and never an implicit search list; resolve a name that contains any dots by first trying it as a fully qualified domain name and, if that fails, with the names in the search list appended; and resolve a name containing no dots by appending the search list right away, while again not using any implicit search list.

To minimise the potential vulnerabilities, the RFC recommends three things: hosts that implement the domain search option SHOULD also implement the search list recommendations of RFC 1536; where DNS parameters such as the domain search list or the DNS servers have been manually configured, these parameters SHOULD NOT be overridden by DHCP; and a host SHOULD require the use of DHCP authentication prior to accepting a domain search option.
sections.plainLanguage: A rogue DHCP server could point your computer at its own DNS server, or at domain names that are not yours, and use the answers to pretend to be someone else's site. Signing the DNS answers does not help, because the rogue server can sign its own records properly. The fix is to require the DHCP exchange itself to be authenticated.

sections.title: Option Codes and Their Origin
sections.content:
IANA has assigned an option code from the DHCP option code space defined in the IANA Considerations section of RFC 3315 to each of the two options: 23 for the DNS Recursive Name Server option and 24 for the Domain Search List option.

The RFC records in its acknowledgements that these options were originally part of the DHCPv6 specification, written by Jim Bound, Mike Carney, Charlie Perkins, Ted Lemon, Bernie Volz and Ralph Droms, and that the analysis of the potential attack through the domain search list is taken from the specification of the DHCPv4 Domain Search option, RFC 3397.
sections.plainLanguage: Each option has a number that identifies it on the wire: 23 for the list of DNS servers and 24 for the domain search list. Both were part of the original DHCPv6 specification before they were split out into this document.
